title: U.S. Commerce Department Rushed to Clear Nvidia H200 Exports to China
summary:
In recent months, Jeffrey Kessler, the official overseeing the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, has pressured staff to expedite the approval of sales of Nvidia’s H200 graphics processing units to China, according to three people with knowledge of the matter. In some cases, Kessler directed staff at BIS —an agency under the Commerce Department—to approve the exports over objections from other U.S. government departments, two of those people said.

The H200, launched in 2023, is an older generation of Nvidia chips that developers can use to train and run AI models. In December 2025, President Donald Trump approved the chip, which is a generation behind Nvidia’s mainstay Blackwell product, for sale to China, after intense lobbying from former CEO Jensen Huang. As part of the approval, Nvidia agreed to give the U.S. government a 25% cut of H200 sales to China.

Botanists, he complained, used “microscopic malice” to reduce the spurs, petals and stamens of his favourite flowers to “obscene processes and prurient apparitions”. Others were less squeamish. In 1908, Marie Stopes, the scientist who later became a champion of birth control, spent three days in Japan’s Matsushima Bay in a state of “grand excitement” hunting ginkgo sperms. Oliver Sacks, the neurologist, passed his adolescence at Kew gawping at the cycads’ sexual organs. Reading Ben Dark’s excellent account, it is hard not to conclude that even the most modest plants are living in a state of permanent arousal.

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. I loved Maurice Sendak’s Where the Wild Things Are. Max’s visit to the land of monsters is escapist, of course, but there’s darkness and poetry in it, too. “The walls became the world all around” has always stuck with me.

The book that changed me as a teenager
A Tree Grows in Brooklyn by Betty Smith. My mom gave it to me at around 12 or 13, and I remember thinking it was such an adult book at the time. It gave me a protagonist to admire who thrived in spite of the setbacks in her life, and also helped put into perspective the charmed life I’d been living.

title: Why Bending Spoons Could Tap Convertible Bonds Next
summary:
Since going public in July, Bending Spoons has tapped the debt and equity markets to raise money mostly to buy more tech firms, and to run its growing portfolio. One financing option the company hasn’t yet used is convertible bonds, but that could make sense soon. 

With interest rates higher now than they have been, the company is considering issuing convertible bonds, as a supplement to its existing financing, a person close to the company said. Convertible bonds generally have lower interest rates than comparable non-convertible debt, because holders get the option to convert into stock, which can dilute existing shareholders. 

Its need for capital is likely to remain intense. title: Anthropic’s IPO Triumph
summary:
Anthropic pulled it off. The biggest pure-play AI company out there, maker of the Claude line of AI models, went public on Thursday, with its shares jumping as much as 39% above its IPO price. The stock settled back a bit to close at $97.17, up 17% from its IPO price. That gave it a market capitalization of $1.76 trillion, assuming you include all options, restricted stock units and convertible notes that might one day become shares. Not bad for a company that’s just five years old.

What makes the IPO even more notable is that it occurred despite months of investor jitters about the cost of AI development. title: BLUF: The OSS Is Back — In Name. The Hard Part Is the Authorities.
summary:
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has given the Pentagon’s top special operations civilian the most storied name in American irregular warfare. Whether the new Office of Strategic Services becomes more than a rebrand — and how it coexists with a CIA that inherited the original OSS’s crown jewels — will be settled on Capitol Hill and in the field, not in a memo.

Bottom Line Up Front

•What changed: A Hegseth memo dated Nov. 2 and released Nov. 12 gives the Assistant Secretary of War for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict (ASW(SO/LIC)) a new title — Assistant Secretary of War for the Office of Strategic Services — raises the post to parity with the service secretaries, and adds money, people and acquisition authority.

•What didn’t: Nothing in the memo touches Title 50, covert action, or the CIA’s statutory lane. The new “OSS” is a civilian oversight and resourcing office for special operations forces.

title: The Future of Nvidia Is About More Than AI Chips
summary:
EXPERT PERSPECTIVE — Nvidia’s board announced that Jensen Huang had resigned 33 years after he co-founded the company.

What happens to a company when a visionary CEO is gone? Too often, innovation fades and the company coasts for years on momentum and its brand. Rarely does it regain its former glory.

That’s the danger facing Nvidia — and the challenge its board must confront.

Huang reinvented Nvidia three times. In 2006, he launched CUDA, turning a graphics chip for PC gamers into a general-purpose computing platform — and funded it for years ahead of any revenue. In 2012, when researchers used Nvidia chips to win the ImageNet contest, he pointed the company toward deep learning. In 2020, with the acquisition of Mellanox, Nvidia went from selling boards with GPUs to selling integrated racks that power AI data centers.

title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr
summary:
Scientific discoveries are effortlessly explained in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by passion

Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work.

But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood.

title: Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe | Rafael Behr
summary:
In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours

In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power”.

Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

title: How JPMorgan, Citi Missed Megaspeed Risks in a $2.8 Billion Data Center Loan
summary:
A Southeast Asian data center boom has attracted billions in financing from major U.S. banks. JPMorgan and Citigroup, for instance, lent money in 2025 to a data center operator that did business with Megaspeed, a company now at the center of the scandal surrounding Nvidia and former CEO Jensen Huang.

Now, as scrutiny of the region’s role in national security intensifies, those loans highlight an emerging risk for banks: indirect exposure to potentially problematic companies through their borrowers. Banks lending to data center operators are typically expected to vet the operators’ major customers, and the financing arrangement raises questions about how thoroughly banks examined complex ownership structures and other potential red flags in Southeast Asia.

Why it matters: Holes in traditional Medicare leave seniors exposed to out-of-pocket costs and affordability struggles, but making the program's benefits more generous may be prohibitively expensive.

The big picture: Democrats scored overwhelming gains in the midterms after making health care affordability a major priority for the next Congress.

title: Push to reinstate Jensen Huang tests superstar tech CEO accountability
summary:

Why it matters: Silicon Valley has long treated its most successful founders as indispensable. But a new class of tech billionaires, led by figures like Elon Musk, has amplified that culture while swatting away efforts to curtail their power.
